passages.text: Muscle weakness is also a common symptom of vitamin D deficiency, further increasing the risk of falls and bone fractures in adults. CONTEXT: It is unclear whether vitamin D supplementation reduces risk of falls, and results from randomized controlled trials (RCTs) are conflicting. OBJECTIVE: The objective of this work is to determine whether 2000 IU/day of supplemental vitamin D3 decreases fall risk. DESIGN: VITamin D and OmegA-3 TriaL (VITAL) is a double-blind, placebo-controlled RCT including 25 871 adults, randomly assigned November 2011 to March 2014 and treated for 5.3 years (median). SETTING: This is a nationwide study.

passages.text: In subgroup analyses, all cause mortality was significantly lower in trials with vitamin D3 supplementation than in trials with vitamin D2 supplementation (P for interaction=0.04); neither vitamin D3 nor vitamin D2 was associated with a statistically significant reduction in all cause mortality. CONCLUSIONS: Vitamin D supplementation alone was not associated with all cause mortality in adults compared with placebo or no treatment. Vitamin D supplementation reduced the risk of cancer death by 16%. synthesis.answer: The evidence mostly argues against routine daily vitamin D supplementation for healthy adults. Large trials in vitamin D-replete adults found no effect on cancer, cardiovascular events, or type 2 diabetes, and no bone density or fall benefit [fbce4d7a6120#3]. The Finnish trial found no lower rate of major cardiovascular events or invasive cancer in older adults [0dafa2c8c11c#3], and VITAL found no reduction in fractures among generally healthy midlife and older adults [d8b33533d51c#3]. A meta-analysis found no all-cause mortality reduction, though cancer death fell by 16% [81282aae0b32#2]. The contradicting side is real but narrower. The Endocrine Society guideline suggests empiric supplementation for adults aged 75 and older for mortality, and for high-risk prediabetes [8279771cfc3d#4]. A BMJ commentary notes that guideline groups still recommend supplementation despite ineffectiveness reviews [9c98e4515e3d#0]. Overall, the supporting evidence is stronger for general adults, with targeted use in specific groups still debated.
synthesis.one_line: Generally no: trials show little benefit for healthy adults, though guidelines suggest targeted use such as in those aged 75 and older or with prediabetes.
